rationale: B wins because it thinks one step closer to the reporter's notebook. The line "whether every store has repair technicians on site or is a drop-off point that ships gear elsewhere" identifies the fact that decides whether the rollout is real infrastructure or just a counter sign. A is strong, but "The contrarian angle is your sharpest and your riskiest" still nudges the founder toward pitching a labor tension that B correctly treats as a defensive answer first.
gaps_in_A: "competitors get benchmarked against" smuggles in a competitive-comparison claim without competitor facts. It is plausible, but plausible is where lazy pitches go to buy a blazer.

"The contrarian angle is your sharpest and your riskiest" overstates the labor play as a proactive pitch. With only "unionization activity at several stores," the smarter move is a prepared answer, not a flamethrower email.
A misses the local bottom-rung version of the rollout. "All 180+ stores" creates city-by-city feature potential if REI can produce a store, a repair worker, and a member.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is a little early unless the missing dividend amount, repair operating model, and union-status facts are pinned down first.
gaps_in_B: "the co-op had its best year for members" overstates the supplied fact. The update says largest-ever dividend, not best year, and B itself knows membership growth could explain the record.
"Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI" is a lively headline, but it invents the tent unless REI confirms tents are accepted. Cute cannot outrun the facts.
"who fixes the zipper" has the same problem: good local color, unsupported repair-category specificity. Keep it as a reporting target, not as a claim.
"Use `newsjack-detector` only if a current retail or resale signal appears" is sound process advice, but it is tool chatter in an angle set. Useful, yes; elegant, no.
